slides.notes: Open the orientation as a method lecture rather than as a preface. The source span is short, but the notebook turns it into a working contract for the whole course: translate each geometric object, visualize the right feature, and record a check. Emphasize that students are learning how to read the remaining notebooks.

Present the three-part rhythm as the course grammar. Translation names the data, visualization chooses a representation that exposes geometry, and checking records an invariant or residual. The repetition is intentional because later topics become less mysterious when the same inspection habit keeps returning.

Make the independence contract explicit. The printed pages and PDF pages provide orientation for topic coverage, but the notebook and deck must stand on their own. Students should not need the source open in order to understand the computational lesson or to rerun its evidence.

Use the diagram to separate four roles that often blur together. Data is how an object is represented, transformations are allowed changes of description, invariants are what should survive, and checks are small tests that keep the visual honest. This distinction will matter immediately for coordinates, frames, forms, and curvature.

Explain functions as reusable rules with declared input and output spaces. In differential geometry, a map is rarely only a formula; it carries domain, target, parameters, and differentiability assumptions. The slide prepares students to ask what the code is allowed to feed into a rule.

Frame sets and maps as bookkeeping for geometry rather than elementary review. A curve, a surface patch, a tangent vector, and a form all belong to different kinds of spaces. When students track those spaces explicitly, many later type errors become mathematical errors they can diagnose.

Slow down on the warning because it is the main habit of the course. A plotted picture can change when coordinates or parameters change, while the geometric quantity of interest may stay fixed. The right question is not whether the drawing is attractive, but what it proves possible to inspect.

Use the concept route map as a preview of dependencies rather than a decorative overview. Euclidean calculus supplies derivatives and measurement, curves make moving frames visible, surfaces add patches and normals, and global structure asks what survives across charts. The inspection target is the flow from local computation to geometric meaning.

Treat the diagnostic geometry artifact as a compact sample of the course method. The point is not to master every later object now, but to see the pattern: a base object is drawn together with the data that measures it. Ask students to identify what would count as a failed diagnostic.

This slide turns the notebook prose into a translation table. A point becomes coordinates, a tangent vector becomes a base point plus direction, a form becomes an evaluator, and curvature becomes measured deviation. The table is deliberately operational so students can map definitions to code variables.

Introduce the interactive model as a laboratory rather than a spectacle. Rotation and parameter changes are useful only when students can name the geometric claim being inspected. The local HTML artifact is a reminder that interaction should sharpen a question, not replace one.

Explain the JSON checks as the audit trail behind the visuals. File existence and nonzero size are basic checks, while symbolic residuals and numerical tolerances record whether a claim survived computation. This is the course safeguard against passive pictures that look plausible but teach little.

Use the failure modes as a practical reading checklist. A tangent vector at the wrong base point, a singular patch, or a sign error in a convention should produce visible or numerical symptoms. Students should learn to welcome these failures because they expose the assumptions behind the definition.

Encourage students to read code cells as part of the mathematical exposition. Variable names are chosen to mirror roles such as tangent vector, patch, form, metric, and residual. The goal is not programming for its own sake; it is to keep every definition close to an executable witness.

Present the applied lab as a controlled perturbation exercise. Students change one parameter, rerun the artifact, and decide which visual features and check values should change. This builds the habit of predicting invariants before trusting a regenerated figure.

The checklist condenses the orientation into questions students can actually use. Each question points to a different source of understanding: spaces, data, transformations, invariants, and failure tests. Returning to this list will make later notebooks feel like variations on a familiar investigation.

Close by returning to the three instincts from the notebook. Every object should have data, every visualization should have an inspection target, and every formula should face a small test. The next lesson can then begin with the same discipline already in place.
